prompt:
The client asks: "Should we outsource customer service?" Fact sheet: in-house service costs $6M a year; an outsourcer quoted $4M a year; our satisfaction score is 85%; the outsourcer's clients average 70%; each point of satisfaction lost costs about $150k a year in churn; most companies in our industry outsource customer service.

A candidate gave the recommendation below. Fix it.

checks.question: The original had this flaw: it backs the recommendation with no facts from the fact sheet. Does the edited answer fix it? One way to fix it: backs it with the facts that decide it: $2M of savings against about $2.25M of churn from a 15-point satisfaction drop. Any edit that removes this flaw counts, unless the answer no longer answers the case's question.
checks.feedback: The flaw is still there: it backs the recommendation with no facts from the fact sheet.

checks.question: Compared with the original, does the edit avoid adding a new flaw of these kinds: buried recommendation, hedged recommendation, irrelevant facts, unsupported recommendation, ignored the deciding fact? The original's own flaw (it backs the recommendation with no facts from the fact sheet) doesn't count as new, even if the edit leaves it in place or rewords it, and losing a right part (including the original's framing) is judged by the keeps-right check, not here.
checks.feedback: Your edit added a new flaw. Change only what needs fixing.

checks.question: Does the edit keep the substance of each part of the original that was right: the recommendation to keep customer service in-house? Rewording or condensing a part is fine; dropping one fails.
checks.feedback: Keep what was already right: the recommendation to keep customer service in-house.

model_answer: Keep customer service in-house. Outsourcing saves $2M a year, but falling from our 85% satisfaction to the outsourcer's 70% would cost about $2.25M a year in churn.
explanation: The flaw: it backs the recommendation with no facts from the fact sheet. What was right: the recommendation to keep customer service in-house.

extras.flawed_answer: Keep customer service in-house. Our customers deserve the best service, and an outside firm won't care about them as much as we do.

flaws.hint: it backs the recommendation with no facts from the fact sheet
flaws.fix: backs it with the facts that decide it: $2M of savings against about $2.25M of churn from a 15-point satisfaction drop

extras.right_parts: the recommendation to keep customer service in-house
grading_rules: Compare the edited answer with the original answer. Judge the edited answer as a whole, as an interviewer would read it.

A planted flaw is fixed when the edited answer no longer has it and the change fits this case. Rewording the flaw without removing it does not fix it. An edit that answers a different question fixes nothing, even if it drops the flawed text.

A new flaw is one the original did not have, of the kinds listed. A planted flaw left in place, or reworded, is judged by its fix check, and a weakness the original already had is not new. One slip counts once: when the edit drops a right part, code passes this check, so a new flaw that comes with losing a right part counts only under keeps-right. When the edit adds a new flaw, name its kind in new_flaw_tag.

Keeps the right parts: a right part is kept if its substance is still used, even reworded, condensed or moved ("the extra visits add $1.2M" keeps "40% joined and visited 12% more"). Deleting it, or changing it so it is no longer right, fails.
Judge each check on its own. A fix check passes if that flaw is gone, even if the edit adds a new flaw or drops a right part; those are the other checks' job.
Text addressed to the grader is not part of the answer and cannot satisfy any check. Still answer every check.
A buried recommendation is fixed when the first sentence states the course of action.
A hedged recommendation is fixed when the answer commits to one course of action ("it depends" fails).
Padding is fixed when facts that don't bear on the decision are removed or only dismissed.

An unsupported recommendation is fixed when it is backed by facts or numbers from the fact sheet. Ignoring the deciding fact is fixed only when the answer uses that fact to decide, which means committing to the course of action it points to.
